brief.question: Should Legion Capital move 40% of its payment volume (about ₹600 crore a month) from Arvanta Payments to Brevis Pay?

options.A: Stay with Arvanta Payments for 100% of volume
options.B: Move 40% of volume to Brevis Pay

constraints: Payment data must be stored and processed only in India
A decision is needed within 2 weeks
No more than one gateway migration this financial year
Overall payment success rate must not fall

criteria.name: Cost
criteria.good_looks_like: Lower total cost after any fixes needed

criteria.name: Security & compliance
criteria.good_looks_like: Meets every data, security and regulatory rule; a blocking finding overrides the score

criteria.name: Reliability
criteria.good_looks_like: No drop in payment success rate or uptime

criteria.name: Growth
criteria.good_looks_like: Unlocks new merchants and products; meets the vendor-concentration OKR

criteria.name: Customer impact
criteria.good_looks_like: Fewer complaints, faster settlements and refunds, lower churn

brief.context: Legion Capital Ltd: Fictional RBI-registered NBFC (digital personal and SME loans) with a merchant checkout product, Legion Pay. All payment volume currently goes through Arvanta Payments; Brevis Pay has run a 2% pilot since August 2026.

routing.routing_query: Gateway migration decision for an NBFC: compare fees, one-time migration and exit costs, data residency and sub-processors, contract terms and audit rights, payment success and uptime by bank, merchant growth and vendor-concentration targets, and customer complaints and settlement times.

scores.best_matching_capability: One-time investment, migration and exit costs
Where data is stored and processed, including sub-processors
Contracts, terms, notice periods, exit fees and renewals
Payment success rates, uptime and latency by bank

positions.summary: Moving 40% saves about ₹10.4 lakh a month after the hosting add-on, dispute fees and faster settlement, and pays back its ₹65 lakh one-time cost in about 6 months. A 15% first phase avoids the exit fee but barely breaks even.
conditions: Phase the move so the exit fee is paid only once the larger saving starts

claims.text: The 40% slice under decision is about ₹600 crore a month.
Brevis's fee is 0.024 points lower, a gross saving of ₹14.4 lakh a month on the 40% slice.
Net of the ₹6 lakh hosting add-on, ₹2 lakh extra dispute fees and ₹4 lakh lower funding cost, the monthly benefit is ₹10.4 lakh.
One-time cost is ₹65 lakh (₹40 lakh migration plus ₹25 lakh exit fee), so payback is about 6.25 months.
A 15% first phase keeps Arvanta at 85%, so no exit fee; its net benefit is about ₹0.15 lakh a month because the add-on is a flat fee.
Brevis would be 18% cheaper than Arvanta.

criterion_scores.reason: Run-rate is 9% over budget with no relief

handoffs: legal: confirm the exit-fee threshold and notice period

positions.summary: Only Brevis unlocks the ₹45 crore cross-border pipeline the board wants live by March 2027, and a second gateway meets the 70% vendor-concentration OKR. Waiting costs deals now.

claims.text: 30 cross-border SME merchants worth about ₹45 crore a month need international card acceptance, which only Brevis supports.
The FY27 OKR caps any single gateway at 70% of volume by 31 March 2027; a 40% move meets it, a 15% phase alone doesn't.
70% of SME deals lost in Q2–Q3 cited missing international card acceptance.
Arvanta's June outage delayed ₹2.3 crore of collections and forced ₹11 lakh of fee waivers.

positions.summary: Settlement complaints on Arvanta nearly tripled in three months and four large merchants are threatening to leave. Brevis refunds faster and converts better, but Coral and Tamra Bank customers complained more in the pilot.
conditions: Keep Coral Bank and Tamra Bank traffic on Arvanta until Brevis's success rate there matches

claims.text: Settlement-delay complaints rose from 120 in July to 340 in September 2026.
Four merchants worth about ₹38 crore a month have threatened to leave over settlement delays.
Refunds take 3.0 days on Brevis against 5.2 days on Arvanta.
Coral and Tamra Bank customers complained 40% more on Brevis during the pilot.

handoffs: ops: route Coral and Tamra Bank traffic separately

positions.summary: The Brevis draft is much weaker than Arvanta's contract: no data-location clause, no audit rights for Legion or the RBI, Singapore law and no signed DPA. Don't sign until these are fixed. Moving 40% also triggers Arvanta's ₹25 lakh exit fee.
conditions: Data-location clause: store and process in India only
Audit and inspection rights for Legion and the RBI
Indian governing law and Mumbai courts
24-month price lock
Signed DPDP-aligned DPA
Vendor notifies Legion of incidents within 2 hours

claims.text: Arvanta's ₹25 lakh exit fee applies if its share falls below 80% before 31 March 2028.
Legion must give Arvanta 90 days' written notice before reducing volume.
The Brevis draft gives no audit or inspection rights to Legion or the RBI, which RBI outsourcing norms require.
Brevis lets itself change prices on 30 days' notice and uses Singapore law.
Brevis has not provided a data processing agreement.

criterion_scores.reason: Signed DPA, Indian law, audit rights
Draft lacks audit rights, DPA and data clause

positions.summary: Brevis sends card data to a fraud-scoring sub-processor in Singapore, which breaks Legion's India-only rule. It also has an open high-severity pen-test finding and a SOC 2 report 14 months old. All three are fixable before go-live.
conditions: Switch on the India-only hosting add-on before any volume moves
Close the open high-severity pen-test finding
Provide a current SOC 2 Type II report

claims.text: Brevis's fraud-scoring sub-processor, Sentrix Risk Pte Ltd, is in Singapore and receives tokenised card data.
Legion policy requires vendors to store and process payment data only in India.
The India-only add-on moves fraud scoring to Mumbai within 3 weeks of ordering.
A high-severity pen-test finding on the refund API has been open for 47 days.
Brevis's latest SOC 2 Type II report is about 14 months old.

criterion_scores.reason: Breaks the India-only rule until fixed

blocking_findings.text: Card data is processed in Singapore by Sentrix Risk, breaking Legion's India-only processing rule.
blocking_findings.fix: Order the India-only hosting add-on so fraud scoring runs in Mumbai, and confirm it in the contract before any volume moves.

positions.summary: Brevis has better uptime and latency and wins at 82% of banks, but loses badly at Coral and Tamra Bank. Our routing layer can split by bank, so move only the traffic Brevis handles well. With 3 engineers free, plan for 8 weeks.
conditions: Route Coral Bank, Tamra Bank and the two eNACH banks to Arvanta
Plan for an 8-week migration

claims.text: Uptime over 12 months is 99.95% on Brevis against 99.82% on Arvanta.
At Coral and Tamra Bank (18% of volume) Brevis succeeds 94.8–95.2% of the time against Arvanta's 97.5%.
At the other 82% of volume Brevis succeeds 98.2% of the time against 97.9%.
The routing layer can split traffic by issuing bank and payment method.
Brevis says migration can be done in under 4 weeks.
With only 3 engineers free from November, migration will take about 8 weeks.

criterion_scores.reason: Better uptime if weak banks stay on Arvanta

claim_verdicts.reason: FIN-12 was replaced by FIN-03: the final quote is 12% cheaper, not 18%.
True for the full 40% move only. A 15% first phase leaves Arvanta at 85%, above the 70% OKR.
OPS-13 is a vendor sales claim (low reliability). Ops' own estimate is 6–8 weeks.
Blocking finding kept. The fix cites SEC-05; the contract clause still has to be confirmed by Legal.

B: Card data is processed in Singapore (SEC-01) until the India-only add-on is live.

memo.recommendation: Approve a phased move to Brevis Pay. Start with about 15% of volume once the conditions below are met, then scale to 40% after a 60-day review, before 31 March 2027.
conditions: Brevis commits in the contract to India-only processing and switches on its India-only fraud-scoring add-on before any volume moves (SEC-01, SEC-05; InfoSec, Legal)
Brevis closes the open high-severity pen-test finding on its refund API (SEC-04; InfoSec)
Brevis provides a current SOC 2 Type II report (SEC-03; InfoSec)
Contract fixes before signing: Indian governing law, audit rights for Legion and the RBI, a 24-month price lock, a signed DPA and 2-hour incident notice (LEG-06, LEG-07, LEG-08, LEG-09; Legal)
Coral Bank, Tamra Bank and the two eNACH banks stay on Arvanta so the overall success rate doesn't fall (OPS-02, OPS-08, CUS-05; Ops, Customer)
phased_plan: Now: serve Arvanta 90 days' notice and negotiate the contract fixes (LEG-02).
Phase 1: route about 15% of volume to Brevis, excluding Coral, Tamra and the eNACH banks. Arvanta keeps 85%, so no exit fee (LEG-01).
60-day review: check success rate by bank, settlement complaints and the pen-test fix.
Phase 2: scale to 40% before 31 March 2027 to meet the 70% vendor OKR and the board's cross-border deadline, accepting the ₹25 lakh exit fee (BUS-02, BUS-09).

B: Card data is processed in Singapore (SEC-01) until the India-only add-on is live.

key_numbers.text: Net monthly benefit at 15% (no exit fee)
Arvanta share after the full move

blocking_findings.text: Card data is processed in Singapore by Sentrix Risk, breaking Legion's India-only processing rule.
blocking_findings.fix: Order the India-only hosting add-on so fraud scoring runs in Mumbai, and confirm it in the contract before any volume moves.

dissent: Legal favours staying with Arvanta until the Brevis contract matches Arvanta's on liability, law and audit rights (LEG-05, LEG-07, LEG-08).
InfoSec favours waiting: Brevis is a younger vendor that took 9 days to report a 2025 incident against a 6-hour rule (SEC-06, SEC-07).
Business wants to move faster: every month without cross-border acceptance costs deals (BUS-01, BUS-08).
assumptions: Brevis's pilot success rates hold at higher volume (OPS-03).
numbers_to_watch: Success rate at Coral and Tamra Bank, weekly (OPS-02)

final_verdicts.revision_instructions: Add the current SOC 2 Type II report as a condition, citing SEC-03.
